source.title: Interpolation can hurt robust generalization even when there is no noise
source.authors: Konstantin Donhauser; Alexandru Tifrea; Michael Aerni; Reinhard Heckel; Fanny Yang

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests an epoch-wise generalization effect by comparing standard risk at early stopping with risk at convergence in adversarially trained linear classification. Its robust-risk results are related but do not test the listed double-descent versions.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses double descent and cites prior results, but its main findings concern adversarially robust risk. Those findings do not measure the risks named by the listed versions. Figure 4b also reports standard risk along a training path and the text says early stopping yields lower standard risk than convergence; it does not establish the full fall-rise-fall shape.
record.test_reason: The paper studies robust overfitting: adversarially robust risk of interpolating versus ridge-regularized or early-stopped linear models, plus shallow networks. It cites double descent as the motivating narrative but does not measure a fall-rise-fall test-error curve along size, epochs or samples. The one standard-risk training-path result (Fig. 4b) only says early stopping beats convergence, and it comes under adversarial training with inconsistent perturbations, which inject about 8% effective label noise. That cannot show epoch-wise double descent, so it does not test V2.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that overparameterized linear models overfit in robust risk even without noise, that ridge regularization and early stopping improve robust generalization, and that ridge biases ℓ∞-adversarial logistic regression toward sparser solutions. A formal proof for early stopping is left to future work.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies adversarially robust risk, regularization, and early stopping in linear regression and logistic regression, plus shallow neural networks; it does not reproduce the original standard-risk double-descent sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The robust-risk outcomes vary with perturbation type and radius, and with whether training perturbations are consistent or inconsistent. The paper also reports almost no regularization benefit for its ℓ2 adversarial-training setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Under ℓ∞ adversarial training at d/n=8, early-stopped gradient descent gives significantly lower standard and robust risk than the converged robust max-margin solution.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In adversarially trained overparameterized linear classifiers, early stopping improves standard and robust risk over the interpolating limit.

fits_no_version.finding: Ridge regularization or early stopping lowers robust risk relative to interpolation, even for noiseless data and d/n well beyond 1, in linear regression, logistic regression and shallow networks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Interpolation causes robust overfitting even without noise in the overparameterized regime.

fits_no_version.finding: Label noise or large inconsistent perturbations prevent interpolation and lower the robust risk of unregularized estimators; optimal ridge still does better. Standard training and ℓ2 adversarial training show no regularization benefit.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Robust-overfitting benefits depend on whether training reaches the robust max-margin interpolator.

record.problems: The neural-network experiment is limited to shallow networks and a sanitized binary MNIST setting; it discards samples based on fitting difficulty and approximates robust test perturbations with 10-step SGD attacks. The paper says a formal proof for early stopping is left for future work and that extending its theory to nonlinear models is unclear. Several plotted comparisons are not given as exact numeric values in the text.

untested.parts: No test-error curve across model sizes in deep networks.
No epoch-wise fall-rise-fall curve of standard test error; Fig. 4b only compares early stopping with convergence under adversarial training.
No sample-size sweep near the interpolation threshold.
Standard-risk curves of min-norm interpolators versus d/n are plotted (Fig. 2) but not analysed as double descent; the focus is robust risk.
No effective-complexity predictor of peak location.
The noise and regularization analysis concerns robust risk. The peak at d=n and its mitigation by regularization are only cited from prior work.

missing.what: Standard-risk curves of the min-ℓ2-norm interpolator versus optimally regularized ridge across d/n, for noisy (σ²=0.2) and noiseless data. These likely show the d=n peak but are figure-only and not discussed. Section 3.3 also states the standard-risk optimum is at λ→0 in the noiseless overparameterized case.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The reader's V2 test link rests on a single early-stopping-versus-convergence comparison under adversarial training; it is downgraded to no test. The paper frames itself as challenging the narrative, drawn from the second descent, that regularization is redundant past interpolation. Its evidence concerns robust risk, a different construct from the test error named by the versions.

versions.untested_parts: No test-error curve across model sizes, or test of a peak near the interpolation size.

The paper compares early stopping with convergence for standard risk, but does not establish the full fall-rise-fall shape over training time; the experiment is adversarially trained linear classification.
No test-error comparison as training sample size increases near an interpolation threshold.
No general double-descent curve across model classes is tested.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location.

The paper examines noise and regularization effects on robust risk, but does not test whether noise or variance drives a double-descent peak, whether peaks split, or whether tuned regularization removes such a peak.
No alternative parameter-count measure or U-shaped re-expression of a second descent is tested.

rows.measure: robust accuracy gain of early-stopped networks over networks at convergence
rows.value: significant gap in favor of the best early-stopped networks; exact values figure only
rows.note: The reported outcome is a robust-accuracy gain, not test error as a function of model size.
rows.check: The measure is the robust-accuracy gain of early stopping over convergence, not test error versus width. The subject is fine, but the operation is mislabelled as scaling: the comparison is early-stopped versus converged.

rows.subject: robust logistic regression
rows.operation_detail: Compared standard risk at early points on the gradient-descent path with risk at convergence.

conditions.value: zero-initialized gradient descent on λ = 0 loss for 5 × 10^5 iterations

rows.measure: standard population risk over training iterations
rows.value: the text reports that early stopping yields a significantly lower standard risk than the converged estimator; exact values figure only
rows.note: This comparison supports early-stopping benefit in the tested setting but does not establish the full fall-rise-fall trajectory.
rows.check: Linked to V2 by the reader. The text reports only that early-stopped GD has lower standard (and robust) risk than the t→∞ robust max-margin solution, under adversarial ℓ∞ training. It gives no fall-rise-fall trajectory and no second descent, and the setting is adversarial training, not ordinary training. This is robust-overfitting / early-stopping evidence, not a test of epoch-wise double descent.

rows.subject: robust logistic regression

rows.value: risk is higher for the interpolating estimator than for an optimal λ > 0 in both perturbation settings; the two settings have comparable robust risks

rows.subject: robust logistic regression

rows.value: the λ = 1 estimator has lower robust risk in the displayed simulations and asymptotic predictions; exact values figure only
rows.note: For small γ, the paper notes that solving the theoretical optimization problem is numerically unstable.

rows.subject: robust logistic regression
rows.operation_detail: Varied the fraction of flipped training labels and compared unregularized and optimally regularized estimators.
rows.baseline: unregularized estimator, λ → 0, at zero label noise
rows.value: moderate label noise lowers the unregularized estimator's robust risk; the optimally regularized estimator still outperforms its unregularized counterpart
rows.uncertainty: standard deviations over five independent dataset draws are shown
rows.note: The paper explicitly says it does not advocate adding artificial label noise.

rows.subject: robust logistic regression
rows.operation_detail: Compared unregularized training with consistent and inconsistent perturbations while varying perturbation radius.
rows.value: for small ε the risks are similar; for large ε, inconsistent perturbation training gives better robust risk
rows.note: The text attributes the large-ε difference to inconsistent perturbations preventing the training loss from vanishing.
